tagline: A farewell letter in Peter's name urging believers to grow in godliness, trust the apostolic witness, reject false teachers, and wait for the day of the Lord.
overview:
Second Peter presents itself as the last words of the apostle Peter, written in the knowledge that his death is near. It has three movements. First, Peter reminds his readers that God's power has given them everything they need for life and godliness, and he urges them to add virtue upon virtue to their faith, grounding his message in what he saw and heard on the mountain of the transfiguration and in the sure word of the prophets. Second, he warns at length against false teachers who will arise within the church, greedy and sensual, promising freedom while enslaved themselves, and he assures readers that God knows how to rescue the godly and judge the wicked, as he did in the flood and at Sodom. Third, he answers scoffers who mock the promise of Christ's coming because nothing seems to change: God is not slow but patient, the day of the Lord will come, and believers look for a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

The letter is short, urgent, and often neglected. It is also among the most debated books of the New Testament, both for its authorship and for its close relationship to the letter of Jude. Its lasting contributions are considerable: a vision of salvation as sharing in the divine nature, one of Scripture's clearest statements about how prophecy came from God, a warning that the church's worst dangers can come from inside it, and a patient answer to the question every generation asks, why the Lord has not yet returned.
author:
The letter claims to come from “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). It refers to Jesus' prediction of Peter's death (1:14; compare John 21:18-19), claims eyewitness presence at the transfiguration (1:16-18), calls itself Peter's second letter (3:1), and names Paul as “our beloved brother” (3:15). The traditional view accepts this at face value.

No New Testament book's authorship has been more questioned, and the doubts are ancient. Eusebius in the fourth century listed 2 Peter among the disputed books, reporting that it had not been received as canonical by all though many had found it useful, and Jerome noted that many rejected it because its style differed from 1 Peter. Modern scholars who judge it pseudonymous, now a large majority of critical scholarship, point to several features: its Greek is ornate and quite unlike 1 Peter; it seems to use Jude; it refers to a collection of Paul's letters and places them alongside the other Scriptures (3:15-16); it speaks of a time when the fathers have died (3:4); and it takes the form of a testament, a farewell speech genre often written in the name of a famous figure after his death. On this view, a follower of Peter wrote in his name to apply his authority to a new crisis, and first readers may have recognized the convention.

Those who defend Petrine authorship respond that Peter may have used a different secretary than Silvanus, or written this letter himself; that the testament form can be used by a real person facing death; that Paul's letters were being copied and gathered early; that the fathers of 3:4 may be the Old Testament patriarchs; and that the early church, which rejected other writings bearing Peter's name, did eventually receive this one. The letter was included in Athanasius's list of New Testament books in AD 367 and has been part of the canon of nearly all churches since.
date: If Peter wrote it, the letter comes shortly before his death in Rome under Nero, most likely around AD 64 to 68, and after 1 Peter. Those who regard it as pseudonymous generally date it between about AD 80 and 130, often in the early second century, making it perhaps the latest book of the New Testament. The relationship to Jude (whose own date is uncertain) and the reference to Paul's letters as a known body of writing are the main factors in the later dating. The earliest surviving manuscript containing it, a papyrus known as P72 from about the third or fourth century, includes 1 and 2 Peter and Jude.
setting:
The letter does not name its readers' location, but it assumes they received Peter's earlier letter (3:1), which would place them among the churches of Asia Minor addressed in 1 Peter, and that they knew some of Paul's letters (3:15-16). They are largely Gentile believers living in a Greek-speaking world. The letter uses vocabulary familiar to Greek moral philosophy, such as virtue, self-control, and godliness, and even speaks of sharing in the divine nature, borrowing the language of its culture to express the gospel.

The pressing danger is internal. Teachers within the churches are denying the Lord's return and future judgment, and are using freedom as a cover for sensual indulgence and greed. Their skepticism about Christ's coming may reflect Greek philosophical doubts about divine intervention in a stable universe (everything continues as it always has, 3:4), and their moral looseness may be a distorted version of Christian freedom. The letter's answer rests on history (God has intervened before, in the flood and at Sodom), on eyewitness testimony, and on the character of God.
purpose: Second Peter aims to secure the readers in the truth they already know. The author says repeatedly that he is reminding them (1:12-15; 3:1-2), so that after his departure they will remember. He wants them to grow in grace and knowledge, to recognize and reject false teachers, and to hold to the promise of Christ's return with holy and patient lives. The letter closes with a summary of its purpose: to be on guard, not carried away by error, and to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
story: Second Peter looks back to the transfiguration, when the Father's voice declared Jesus his beloved Son, and further back to the flood, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the prophet Balaam. It looks forward to the end of the story, the day of the Lord, the dissolving of the present heavens and earth, and a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells, a hope drawn from Isaiah 65-66 and developed in Revelation 21-22. Within the New Testament it reflects the transition from the apostolic generation to the churches that must carry on after the apostles have died, relying on the apostles' writings and the prophetic Scriptures.
christ: Second Peter's opening calls Jesus “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1), one of the New Testament's plainest statements of his deity, and the letter repeatedly names him Lord and Savior. The transfiguration stands at its center: the apostles saw his majesty and heard the Father say, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (1:17). Christ's coming in power is the hope the false teachers deny and the letter defends, and the knowledge of Christ is the source of all growth in godliness. The false teachers are condemned precisely for “denying the Master who bought them” (2:1), a phrase that presents Christ as the Lord who purchased his people. The letter ends with a doxology addressed to Christ himself.
reading:
Read 2 Peter as a farewell testament: a leader facing death gathers what matters most and passes it on. Chapter 1 is its positive heart, chapter 2 its sustained warning, chapter 3 its defense of hope. Chapter 2 is full of vivid denunciation, which can feel harsh, but it serves the protection of vulnerable believers from teachers who exploit them.

Reading 2 Peter alongside Jude is illuminating. Jude 4-18 and 2 Peter 2:1-3:3 share much of their content, order, and imagery: false teachers who deny the Master, the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, Balaam, waterless springs and clouds, and scoffers in the last days. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude, because Jude's version is more compact and vivid, and because 2 Peter omits Jude's references to Jewish writings outside the Old Testament (1 Enoch and the dispute over Moses' body). Others argue Jude used 2 Peter, noting that 2 Peter predicts the false teachers in the future tense while Jude says the apostles foretold them; still others propose a common source. Borrowing between inspired writers would not have troubled ancient readers. Watch also for the letter's careful account of prophecy (1:19-21) and its famous saying that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years (3:8), which is about God's patience, not a formula for calculating dates.

structure.title: Growing in godliness
structure.summary: After the greeting, Peter reminds readers that God has given them everything for life and godliness, calls them to add virtue to faith, and explains that he writes as a reminder before his death.

structure.title: Eyewitness and prophetic testimony
structure.summary: The apostles did not follow clever myths: they saw Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word came from God as men were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

structure.title: False teachers and their judgment
structure.summary: False teachers will arise, as false prophets did in Israel. God judged fallen angels, the ancient world, and Sodom while rescuing Noah and Lot, and he will judge these greedy and sensual teachers.

structure.title: The day of the Lord
structure.summary: Scoffers deny Christ's coming, but God's word created and judged the world, God is patient, and the day will come. Believers wait in holiness for a new heaven and earth and grow in grace and knowledge.

themes.title: Knowledge of God and Christ
themes.body: Knowledge runs through the letter, from the greeting (1:2) to the final charge (3:18). It is not esoteric information of the kind false teachers claimed, but personal, growing acquaintance with Christ that produces a godly life. Knowledge that yields no fruit, the letter warns, leaves a person nearsighted and forgetful.

themes.title: Growth in virtue
themes.body: The chain of virtues in 1:5-7, from faith to love, shows the Christian life as active growth grounded in God's gift. God's power has already given what is needed; believers respond by making every effort. The aim is a life that confirms one's calling and election and ends in a rich welcome into Christ's eternal kingdom.

themes.title: The reliability of the apostolic and prophetic word
themes.body: Against teachers who dismissed Christ's return as myth, 2 Peter appeals to two witnesses: the apostles who saw Christ's glory, and the prophets whose words came from God by the Spirit. The letter also places Paul's letters beside the other Scriptures, an early sign of the church recognizing its apostolic writings.

themes.title: Judgment and rescue
themes.body: Chapter 2 traces a double pattern through Genesis: God judges the ungodly and rescues the righteous, as he judged the ancient world and saved Noah, and destroyed Sodom and delivered Lot. The pattern assures believers that God's judgment on false teachers is certain and that he knows how to rescue his own.

themes.title: Patience and the coming day
themes.body: The apparent delay of Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the present order will give way to a new heaven and a new earth. The right response is holy and godly living, eager expectation, and peace.

keyChapters.why: God's provision for life and godliness, the ladder of virtues, the transfiguration testimony, and the classic statement on how prophecy came from God.
The longest New Testament warning against false teachers, closely parallel to Jude.
The answer to scoffers about Christ's delayed return, the promise of a new heaven and earth, and the reference to Paul's letters as Scripture.
